topic: Quad strain in sprinting and kicking

slides.headline: Felt a grab in your thigh mid-sprint?
slides.sub: Quad strains are common in summer sport. Here's how they usually settle.

slides.title: Why the front of the thigh goes
slides.body: Sprinting, kicking and sudden changes of pace ask the quads to lengthen and contract hard at once. A strain often shows up as a sharp grab, then tightness and pain on stretching.

slides.title: The first few days: keep it calm
slides.body: Walk within comfort, avoid stretching hard into the pain, and skip sprinting or kicking for now. Gentle movement usually helps more than complete rest or pushing through.

slides.title: Load it early, but gradually
slides.body: Light exercises like isometric holds, bridges and partial squats can start once walking feels easier. The aim is to build strength without flaring it up the next day.

slides.title: Kicking and sprinting come last
slides.body: Running builds from jogging to strides before full sprints. Kicking starts with short, light passes. Rushing this stage is one common reason strains come back.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A pop with heavy bruising, a visible dent in the thigh, trouble walking, or pain that keeps getting worse is worth an assessment sooner rather than later.

topic: Massage for the side of the thigh (ITB)

slides.headline: Can you really 'release' your ITB?
slides.sub: What massage does for the outside of your thigh, and what it doesn't.

slides.title: The ITB is tough, not stuck
slides.body: The iliotibial band is a thick, strong strip of connective tissue. It isn't designed to stretch much, so massage won't lengthen it. What it can do is ease tension in the muscles around it.

slides.title: Where we actually work
slides.body: A remedial massage therapist will often spend time on the glutes, the muscle at the front of the hip (TFL), the quads and the hamstrings. These are often where the tightness is felt most.

slides.title: Firm doesn't need to mean brutal
slides.body: Pressure on the side of the thigh can feel intense. Most people get more out of steady, comfortable pressure than gritting their teeth. Tell your therapist if it's too much.

slides.title: Pair it with strength
slides.body: Massage can help the area feel looser for a while. Hip and glute strengthening, plus sensible changes to your running or riding load, are usually what keep it feeling that way.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Sharp pain on the outside of the knee during runs, swelling, or pain that keeps building despite rest is worth a physio assessment alongside your massage.

slides.headline: Outer thigh feeling like rope?
slides.body: Our remedial massage therapists work through the hips and thighs, then suggest simple things to keep it moving between sessions. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Can massage really 'release' your ITB? Not quite, and that's fine.

The iliotibial band is a thick, strong band of tissue down the outside of the thigh. It doesn't stretch much, so no amount of pressure will lengthen it. What massage can do is ease tension in the muscles that attach to it and sit around it: the glutes, the front of the hip, the quads and the hamstrings.

Steady, comfortable pressure usually beats gritting your teeth. And massage tends to work well alongside hip and glute strength plus sensible changes to your training load.

Sharp outer-knee pain on runs or swelling is worth a physio check.

topic: Back to work after the break: five body checks

slides.headline: Back at work? Run these five checks
slides.sub: A quick audit for your body in your first week back.

slides.title: 1. How's your desk set up?
slides.body: Screen at eye level, feet on the floor, keyboard close enough that your elbows rest by your sides. If things got moved over the break, a five-minute reset is worth it.

slides.title: 2. How often do you move?
slides.body: Holidays usually mean more walking and less sitting. Back at work, that flips overnight. Aim to stand or walk every 30 to 45 minutes, even briefly.

slides.title: 3. How's your commute?
slides.body: Heavy laptop bag on one shoulder? Long drive with the seat reclined? Small changes like a backpack or a lumbar roll can make the first weeks feel easier.

slides.title: 4. Any holiday niggles hanging on?
slides.body: A sore knee from beach walks or a stiff back from the long drive home often settles. If it's still there after a couple of weeks, it's worth getting it looked at.

slides.title: 5. Is exercise in the calendar?
slides.body: Book it in like a meeting. Two or three short sessions a week is a good starting point, and much easier to keep than an ambitious plan you drop by February.

topic: Pain at the back of the heel from shoes

slides.headline: New shoes rubbing the back of your heel?
slides.sub: When the heel counter becomes the problem, and what usually helps.

slides.title: Pressure is often the trigger
slides.body: A stiff or high heel counter can press on the back of the heel and the base of the Achilles. Work shoes, new sneakers and summer sandals with a back strap are common culprits.

slides.title: Change the shoes first
slides.body: Swap to shoes with a softer or lower back for a week or two. Some people cut a small notch in the heel tab of old runners, or pad around the sore spot.

slides.title: Try a small heel raise
slides.body: A heel lift or shoes with a slightly higher heel can take some pressure off the base of the Achilles. It's often a helpful short-term step while things settle.

slides.title: Skip deep stretches off a step
slides.body: Dropping your heel off a step can squeeze the sore area. Calf raises on flat ground are usually a better starting point, building up gradually over a few weeks.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A lump that keeps growing, redness and heat, swelling after a fall, or pain that stops you walking normally is worth a proper assessment by a physio.

slides.headline: Heel still sore after the swap?

New work shoes giving the back of your heel a hard time?

topic: Hamstring control, not just flexibility

slides.headline: Still tight after all that stretching?
slides.sub: That tight feeling may be asking for control, not more length.

slides.title: Tight doesn't always mean short
slides.body: Hamstrings can feel tight because they're working hard to protect or stabilise, not because they're too short. Stretching helps some people, but often the feeling comes straight back.

slides.title: Control means strength at length
slides.body: Hamstrings need to stay strong as they lengthen, like when you bend forward or sprint. Clinical Pilates trains this with slow, controlled movement on the reformer and mat.

slides.title: Start with bridges
slides.body: Bridging with your feet on the reformer bar or a box works the hamstrings with your pelvis supported. Slow lowering builds control. Ten steady reps beats thirty rushed ones.

slides.title: Add single-leg work
slides.body: Single-leg bridges, hamstring curls on the reformer and hinging patterns challenge each side separately. It's common to notice one side feels less steady than the other.

slides.title: Keep the stretch, if you like it
slides.body: There's nothing wrong with stretching if it feels good. Pairing it with strength and control work two or three times a week tends to give a longer-lasting change.

slides.headline: Want hamstrings that hold up?
slides.body: Our Pilates team will look at how your hamstrings move and build a program to match your sport or day. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Stretching your hamstrings every day and they still feel tight?

Tightness isn't always about length. Hamstrings often feel tight when they're working hard to protect or stabilise, and stretching alone may only give a short break from that feeling.

Clinical Pilates focuses on control: keeping the hamstrings strong as they lengthen. Bridges with slow lowering, reformer hamstring curls, single-leg work and hinging patterns are a good starting point. Most people notice one side feels less steady than the other at first.

If you enjoy stretching, keep it. Adding strength and control work two or three times a week tends to give a change that lasts longer.

topic: First week back at the desk: ease your neck in

slides.headline: Eight-hour desk days again? Ease in
slides.sub: Your neck had weeks off screens. Give it a few days to catch up.

slides.title: Why week one can feel rough
slides.body: Over the break, your neck moved more and sat still less. Jumping straight back into long screen days asks a lot. Some stiffness in the first week is common and usually settles.

slides.title: Break up the long stretches
slides.body: For the first week, aim for a short move every 30 minutes: look left and right, tuck your chin gently, roll your shoulders. Then stretch the gaps out as you settle.

slides.title: Check your laptop height
slides.body: Working off a laptop on the desk pulls your gaze down. A riser or a few books, plus a separate keyboard and mouse, keeps your eyes level with the top of the screen.

slides.title: Keep some holiday movement
slides.body: That morning walk or swim you did over the break? Keep a shorter version going before or after work. General movement often helps necks tolerate desk time better.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain running into the arm, pins and needles, hand weakness, or headaches that keep building are worth an assessment rather than waiting it out for weeks.

topic: Gaming marathons: your neck and back

slides.headline: Gaming all weekend? Your neck noticed
slides.sub: Long sessions are fine. Staying frozen for hours is the tricky part.

slides.title: It's the stillness, not the game
slides.body: Hours in one position, head forward, shoulders up and wrists busy, can leave the neck and back stiff. Any posture held for too long tends to get uncomfortable.

slides.title: Use the natural breaks
slides.body: Loading screens, respawns and the end of a match are perfect cues. Stand up, look over each shoulder, reach your arms overhead. Thirty seconds adds up across a session.

slides.title: Bring the screen to you
slides.body: Sit back in your chair with the screen at eye level and an arm's length away. If you game from the couch, a cushion behind your lower back and the controller resting on a pillow helps.

slides.title: Balance it with movement
slides.body: A walk, a gym session or a swim on gaming days gives your back and neck a different load. Most people find they stiffen up less when they move more overall.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain spreading into an arm or leg, pins and needles, numbness, or stiffness that isn't easing after a few days of moving more is worth an assessment.

Gaming marathon over the weekend and your neck is paying for it? 🎮

topic: Heat, ice and massage: what pairs well

slides.headline: Heat pack before massage, or ice after?
slides.sub: How to pair heat, cold and massage so they work together.

slides.title: Warmth before often helps
slides.body: A warm shower or heat pack before a remedial massage can help tight muscles feel easier to work on. Many people find they relax into the session faster.

slides.title: After: go with what feels good
slides.body: Most people simply enjoy a warm shower after a massage. Ice isn't usually needed unless an area feels hot or irritated. Neither is essential for the massage to be useful.

slides.title: Fresh injury? Skip deep massage
slides.body: In the first couple of days after a knock or sprain, cold and gentle movement tend to suit better than firm massage on the area. Your therapist can work elsewhere instead.

slides.title: Cold plunges and recovery
slides.body: Ice baths are popular in summer. They can feel refreshing, but research suggests they don't add much for most people's day-to-day recovery. Use them if you enjoy them.

slides.title: Movement ties it together
slides.body: Heat, cold and massage can all ease how muscles feel for a while. Regular movement and strength work are what help that relief stick between sessions.

slides.headline: Want a plan for recovery?
slides.body: Our remedial massage therapists can tailor your session and suggest simple heat, cold and movement ideas to use at home. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Heat pack before your massage, ice afterwards, or neither?

Here's a simple way to think about it. Warmth before a remedial massage, like a warm shower or heat pack, often helps tight muscles relax so the session feels easier. Afterwards, go with what feels good. Most people just enjoy a warm shower, and ice usually isn't needed.

The exception is a fresh knock or sprain. For the first couple of days, gentle movement and cold tend to suit better than deep massage on that spot.

Cold plunges are everywhere this summer. Enjoy them if you like them, but they aren't essential for recovery.

topic: Hot-desking at a new office: a quick setup

slides.headline: Hot-desking? A two-minute setup
slides.sub: New desk every day? Here's a quick routine to make it yours.

slides.title: Chair first, always
slides.body: Raise or lower the seat so your feet sit flat and your hips are level with or a little above your knees. Slide back so the backrest supports you.

slides.title: Then the screen
slides.body: Bring the monitor about an arm's length away with the top near eye level. If you're on a laptop, use a riser and a spare keyboard if the office has them.

slides.title: Keyboard and mouse close
slides.body: Pull them in so your elbows rest near your sides. Reaching forward all day loads the shoulders and upper back more than most people notice.

slides.title: Pack a small kit
slides.body: A compact laptop stand and a lumbar cushion fit in most bags. Having your own setup ready makes it far easier to get comfortable at any desk.

slides.title: When to get it checked

topic: Ankles that keep rolling: rebuilding stability

slides.headline: Why does that ankle keep rolling?
slides.sub: Repeat sprains are common. Rebuilding balance and strength usually helps.

slides.title: Why it happens again
slides.body: After a sprain, the ankle can lose some strength and some of its sense of position. If rehab stops when the pain does, the ankle may not react as quickly next time.

slides.title: Balance is trainable
slides.body: Start by standing on one leg for 30 seconds. Then try it with your eyes closed, on a cushion, or while turning your head. Do it while brushing your teeth.

slides.title: Strengthen the calf and sides
slides.body: Single-leg calf raises and resistance band work for the outside of the ankle build support. A few sets most days, built up over several weeks, is a good starting point for most people.

slides.title: Add hops and direction changes
slides.body: Once balance and strength feel solid, small hops, side-to-side jumps and soft landing drills help prepare the ankle for sport, uneven paths and summer beach runs.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Not being able to put weight on it, bony tenderness, a sense the ankle gives way often, or swelling that won't settle is worth an assessment.

slides.headline: Tired of rolling the same ankle?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios assess your balance, strength and hop control, then build a stability program. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Rolled the same ankle again? It's a really common pattern.

After a sprain, the ankle can lose some strength and some of its sense of where it is. If rehab stops as soon as the pain fades, it may not react as quickly when you step on an uneven path or land awkwardly.

The good news is that balance and strength are trainable. Start with single-leg balance while brushing your teeth, add single-leg calf raises and band work, then progress to hops and side-to-side drills over several weeks.

Trouble taking weight, bony tenderness or frequent giving way are worth getting checked.

topic: Pilates when you have sciatica

slides.title: Start with what feels easy
slides.body: Early sessions often focus on breathing, gentle pelvic tilts and supported positions like lying on your back with knees bent. The aim is to find movement your leg tolerates today.

slides.title: Expect the plan to change
slides.body: Some days you'll do more, some days less. Your instructor adjusts springs, range and positions as symptoms shift, and gradually builds strength through the hips, trunk and legs.

slides.title: When to get it checked first
slides.body: Numbness around the groin or saddle area, changes to bladder or bowel control, or weakness that keeps getting worse need prompt medical attention before any exercise program.

topic: Rotator cuff tears after 50: exercise often comes first

slides.headline: Told you have a rotator cuff tear?
slides.sub: After 50, a tear is common and exercise is often the first step.

slides.title: Tears are common with age
slides.body: Research suggests many people over 50 have some rotator cuff tearing without any pain at all. So a tear on its own doesn't always explain your sore shoulder or decide what happens next.

slides.title: Why exercise usually comes first
slides.body: For many age-related tears, current guidelines recommend a structured exercise program as a first option. Strengthening the muscles around the shoulder often improves pain and function over a few months.

slides.title: What the program looks like
slides.body: Usually it starts with gentle range and isometric holds, then builds to band and weight work for the cuff, shoulder blade and upper back. Two to three sessions a week is a common rhythm.

slides.title: Give it a fair trial
slides.body: Shoulders tend to improve slowly. Many programs run around three months before progress is judged properly. Tracking things like reaching overhead or sleeping on that side shows change better than daily pain.

slides.title: When to get it checked sooner
slides.body: A sudden loss of strength after a fall or heavy lift, being unable to lift your arm at all, or a hot, swollen shoulder should be assessed promptly by your physio or GP.

topic: 30, 45 or 60 minutes: choosing your massage length

slides.headline: 30, 45 or 60 minutes: which to book?
slides.sub: Match the length to the job, not the habit.

slides.title: 30 minutes: one area, focused
slides.body: Good for a single region, like tight shoulders after a desk week or calves after a run. Your therapist can spend real time there without rushing. Ideal if you're fitting it into a lunch break.

slides.title: 45 minutes: two connected areas
slides.body: Handy when things link up, like neck and upper back, or lower back and hips. There's time to work both properly plus a quick check of how they're moving together.

slides.title: 60 minutes: a fuller session
slides.body: Useful for your first visit, when several areas are bothering you, or during heavy training. It leaves room for a proper chat, assessment and work across more of the body.

slides.title: Longer isn't automatically better
slides.body: More time on one sore spot doesn't always help more. Most people find the right length is the one they can book consistently, alongside the exercise and movement that keep them feeling good.

topic: The hip hinge: a lift worth learning

slides.headline: One movement that makes lifting easier
slides.sub: The hip hinge, broken down step by step.

slides.title: What a hip hinge actually is
slides.body: Hinging means bending mainly from the hips, pushing them back while your chest tips forward. It's the pattern behind picking up a box, lifting a suitcase or getting the washing out of the basket.

slides.title: Try the dowel drill
slides.body: Hold a broomstick along your back, touching your head, upper back and tailbone. Push your hips back with soft knees. If the stick stays in contact at all three points, you're hinging.

slides.title: Feel it in your hamstrings
slides.body: As you hinge, you should feel a stretch building in the back of your thighs. Stop there, then squeeze your glutes and stand tall. Most people only need a modest depth to start.

slides.title: Your back can still round a bit
slides.body: Spines are built to bend, and a little rounding is normal. The hinge simply shares the load with your hips and legs, which can make lifting feel easier, especially when you're tired.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Back pain with leg pain, numbness or weakness, or pain that stops you lifting everyday objects is worth an assessment rather than pushing through drills on your own.

topic: Nordic walking with poles

slides.title: What Nordic walking is
slides.body: You walk with two specially designed poles, planting each one behind you and pushing back as you stride. It turns a regular walk into a light full-body session using your arms, shoulders and trunk.

slides.title: Who it often suits
slides.body: People easing back after knee or hip niggles, those with back pain who like walking, and anyone wanting a bit more effort without running. Many people say the poles help them feel steadier too.

slides.title: Getting the poles right
slides.body: Standing with the pole tip beside your foot, your elbow should sit near a right angle. Plant the pole level with your opposite heel and push back, keeping your grip relaxed.

slides.title: Start shorter than you think
slides.body: Your shoulders and upper back may feel it at first. Begin with 15 to 20 minutes on flat ground, early morning or evening to dodge the summer heat, and build up gradually.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Joint pain that builds walk after walk, a swollen knee or ankle, chest discomfort or unusual breathlessness are worth getting checked by your GP or physio before adding more.

topic: Good pain vs bad pain during exercise

slides.headline: Is this ache okay or not?
slides.sub: A simple traffic-light guide for exercise pain.

slides.title: Some discomfort is expected
slides.body: When you load muscles and tendons, a bit of ache is common, especially when starting something new. It doesn't mean you're hurting yourself. Your body is adapting to a new demand.

slides.title: Green light: keep going
slides.body: An ache up to about 3 out of 10 that stays steady during exercise and settles by the next morning is usually fine. Carry on with the plan and progress gradually.

slides.title: Amber light: adjust the dose
slides.body: Pain climbing to 4 or 5 out of 10, or lingering into the next day, is a cue to tweak something. Reduce the weight, range or reps for a session or two, then build back.

slides.title: Red light: stop and check
slides.body: Sharp or stabbing pain, pain that changes how you move, swelling, giving way, or numbness and tingling means stop that exercise and get it assessed before going again.

slides.title: Track it for a week
slides.body: Jot down your pain score during the session and the next morning. Patterns show up quickly, and they help your practitioner adjust your program with much more precision.

slides.headline: Not sure where your pain sits?

topic: The 'slipped disc' myth

slides.headline: Discs don't actually slip out
slides.sub: Why the 'slipped disc' idea causes more worry than it should.

slides.title: Discs are firmly attached
slides.body: Spinal discs are tough, fibrous structures anchored to the bones above and below. They can bulge or irritate nearby nerves, but they can't slide out of place like a dropped plate.

slides.title: Bulges often settle
slides.body: Research suggests disc bulges and herniations often shrink or settle over time as the body reabsorbs them. Most people with disc-related back or leg pain improve without needing anything invasive.

slides.title: The word can make it worse
slides.body: Believing something has 'slipped out' often leads to fear of bending and moving. That guarding tends to make backs stiffer and more sensitive, which can slow the recovery down.

slides.title: What usually helps
slides.body: Staying gently active, walking, short bouts of comfortable movement through the day, and gradually building strength. Your physio can find positions that ease symptoms and set a realistic plan.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Numbness in the saddle area, changes to bladder or bowel control, or leg weakness that keeps getting worse need urgent medical attention. Ongoing leg pain or pins and needles is worth an assessment.

topic: Pilates for ankle stability

slides.headline: Ankles rolling more than they should?

slides.title: Why ankles feel unsteady
slides.body: After a sprain or two, ankles can lose some strength and some of their sense of position. That's often why they feel wobbly on uneven ground, even once the pain has gone.

slides.title: Footwork on the reformer
slides.body: Pressing through the balls of your feet, heels and arches against spring resistance builds calf and foot strength. Your instructor watches that your knee and ankle stay lined up as you work.

slides.title: Slow heel raises and lowers
slides.body: Rising up and lowering down over three to four seconds, first on two feet then one, builds control through the range. Holding a bar or wall at first is completely fine.

slides.title: Balance, then add a challenge
slides.body: Single-leg standing, then eyes closed, a cushion underfoot, or arm movements. Short, regular practice tends to work well. A minute or two a day is a good starting point.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Ankles that keep giving way, swelling that returns after activity, clicking with pain, or pain you can't put weight on after a twist are worth a physio assessment.

topic: Why a sneeze can set off back pain

slides.title: Why a sneeze can do it
slides.body: A sneeze is a fast, forceful contraction of your trunk muscles, often while you're slightly bent or twisted. If your back is already tired, stiff or sensitive, that sudden load can trigger a spasm.

slides.title: It's usually the last straw
slides.body: The sneeze is often the trigger rather than the whole story. Long sitting, poor sleep, a busy week or a lot of lifting can leave your back more sensitive beforehand.

slides.title: What tends to help early
slides.body: Keep gently moving within comfort, try short walks, and change positions often. Heat can ease muscle guarding. Most acute back pain settles noticeably over days to a few weeks.

slides.title: Brace for the next one
slides.body: Feel a sneeze coming? Stand tall, soften your knees, and put a hand on a bench or wall. Avoiding a bent, twisted position can make the next sneeze far less dramatic.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain spreading down a leg with numbness or weakness, saddle numbness, bladder or bowel changes, or pain with fever or unexplained weight loss need prompt medical attention.

topic: Buttock pain and the piriformis: what's really going on

slides.headline: A pain in the backside after the break?
slides.sub: Sore buttock, maybe a tight piriformis. Here's the fuller picture.

slides.title: Piriformis gets blamed a lot
slides.body: The piriformis is a small muscle deep in the buttock. It often gets the blame for buttock pain, but the gluteal tendons, the hip joint and the lower back can all refer pain there too.

slides.title: Sitting is a common trigger
slides.body: Long drives, low couches and back-to-back meetings can all load the buttock. If it grumbles after sitting, try standing up every 30 minutes and avoid sitting on a wallet or phone.

slides.title: Stretching isn't the whole answer
slides.body: A gentle stretch can feel good for a while, but most people do better when they also build strength. Bridges, side-lying leg lifts and step-ups are a good starting point.

slides.title: Ease back into running and hills
slides.body: If the pain started after a big summer of walking or running, trim hills, stairs and pace for a couple of weeks, then build up gradually rather than stopping completely.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain spreading below the knee, pins and needles, numbness, leg weakness, or changes to bladder or bowel control are worth an assessment promptly rather than waiting it out.

topic: Wrist-friendly Pilates modifications

slides.headline: Wrists hate planks? Pilates can adapt

slides.title: Why wrists complain in Pilates
slides.body: Planks, quadruped work and some reformer moves put the wrist in full extension while bearing weight. If your wrists aren't used to it, they often let you know.

slides.title: Try fists or forearms
slides.body: Coming onto your forearms or making a soft fist keeps the wrist straighter. Most mat exercises still work your trunk just as well in these positions.

slides.title: Spread the load through the hand
slides.body: Press through the base of your fingers and the pad of your thumb, not just the heel of the hand. A folded towel under the heel can also ease the angle.

slides.title: Build tolerance gradually
slides.body: Short holds on hands and knees, gentle wrist circles and easy weight shifts can build capacity over a few weeks. Start with what feels comfortable and add a little each time.

slides.title: Tell your instructor early
slides.body: Let your Pilates instructor know at the start of class. They can swap exercises or set up the reformer so you can keep training without wrist pain.

slides.headline: Told your pelvis is 'out'?
slides.sub: Pelvises don't pop out of place. Here's what's more likely going on.

slides.title: Your pelvis is very stable
slides.body: The sacroiliac joints are held by some of the strongest ligaments in the body. They move only a few millimetres, so a pelvis slipping 'out' in daily life is very unlikely.

slides.title: Small differences are normal
slides.body: Most people have small differences from side to side in their pelvis and legs. Research suggests these differences usually don't match up with who has pain.

slides.title: So what is the pain?
slides.body: Pain around the pelvis or lower back is often sensitive joints, muscles or tendons that have been overloaded. It usually settles with the right mix of movement and load.

slides.title: Where adjustments fit in
slides.body: Our chiropractors may use adjustments or soft tissue work to ease pain and help you move. They're one tool, used alongside exercise, not a way to put anything back.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain after a fall or accident, pain in pregnancy, numbness, leg weakness, fever with back pain, or changes to bladder or bowel control are worth an assessment promptly.

slides.headline: Want a clearer explanation?
slides.body: Our chiropractors at Hybrid Physiotherapy assess how you move, explain what's going on and give you exercises to keep you moving. Book online — link in bio.

topic: Rowing machine technique for a happy back

slides.headline: Rowing machine leaving your back sore?
slides.sub: Technique tweaks that make the erg kinder to your back.

slides.title: Legs, body, arms
slides.body: The drive should start with a strong leg push, then a hinge back from the hips, then the arms finish. Pulling with your arms first puts more strain on your back.

slides.title: Hinge, don't slump
slides.body: Keep a tall chest and tip from the hips rather than rounding through the lower back. Imagine sitting up proud, especially when you're tired late in a session.

slides.title: Lower the damper setting
slides.body: A high damper feels heavier, not better, and can tire your back sooner. Most people do well around the middle setting, which lets you focus on smooth, powerful strokes.

slides.title: Build volume gradually
slides.body: Jumping into long sessions after the break is a common trigger. Start with shorter pieces and add five minutes each week as your back adapts.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Back pain spreading into the leg, pins and needles, numbness, or pain that keeps building despite rest is worth an assessment rather than pushing through.

slides.headline: Want a smoother stroke?
slides.body: Our Chatswood physios can watch your technique, check how your back and hips move, and help you build up safely. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Back feeling sore after a few sessions on the rowing machine?

The erg is a great full-body workout, but technique matters. Most back flare-ups come from pulling with the arms first, slumping through the lower back, cranking the damper up or doing too much too soon.

Try this: legs, then body, then arms on the drive, hinge from the hips with a tall chest, keep the damper around the middle, and add about five minutes each week. Pain spreading into the leg, numbness or pain that keeps building is worth getting checked.

topic: Fitting rehab into a busy week

slides.headline: Back at work and rehab's slipped?
slides.sub: How to keep your exercises going in a full week.

slides.title: Shorter sessions still count
slides.body: Ten focused minutes most days often beats one long session you keep skipping. Ask your practitioner which two or three exercises matter most right now.

slides.title: Stack exercises onto habits
slides.body: Do calf raises while the kettle boils, a few squats before your shower, or a stretch after brushing your teeth. Linking exercises to daily routines makes them easier to remember.

slides.title: Plan your week on Sunday
slides.body: Pop rehab into your calendar like a meeting. Choose specific days and times, and have a short version ready for the days that get away from you.

slides.title: Make it easy to start
slides.body: Keep a band near your desk or a mat by the bed. Removing small barriers makes it much more likely that you'll actually do the exercises.

slides.title: Tell us what's realistic
slides.body: If your program doesn't fit your life, tell our team. We'd rather adjust it to something you can stick with than give you a plan you can't keep up.

slides.headline: Need a plan that fits?
slides.body: Our team at Hybrid Physiotherapy builds rehab around your schedule, with programs you can do at home, at work or at the gym. Book online — link in bio.

topic: Massage and posture: what it can and can't change

slides.headline: Can massage change your posture?
slides.sub: An honest look at what massage does and doesn't do.

slides.title: What massage can do
slides.body: Massage can ease muscle tension, help you feel less stiff and make moving more comfortable. Many people find it helps them relax and sleep better after a long week.

slides.title: What it doesn't change
slides.body: Massage doesn't reshape your spine or change how you stand for good. Your resting posture is mostly habit, comfort and the shape your body naturally has.

slides.title: Posture isn't the enemy
slides.body: Research suggests there's no single correct posture for everyone. Staying in any one position for too long is usually the bigger issue, so changing position often through the day matters most.

slides.title: Pair it with movement
slides.body: Massage works well alongside regular movement breaks and strength work for your upper back and shoulders. That combination often helps long desk days feel easier and less stiff by the end of the week.

slides.title: When to see a physio
slides.body: Pain spreading into the arm, pins and needles in the hands, headaches that keep building, or neck and back pain that isn't settling after a few weeks is worth a physio assessment.

topic: Skipping rope: go easy on your calves and shins

slides.headline: Picked up the skipping rope again?
slides.sub: Skipping is great cardio. Here's how to keep calves and shins happy.

slides.title: Why skipping loads your legs
slides.body: Every jump asks your calves, Achilles and shins to absorb and push off. Hundreds of jumps add up quickly, especially if your legs aren't used to it.

slides.title: Start with short rounds
slides.body: Try 30 seconds on, 30 seconds off for five to ten minutes. Add a little time each week rather than jumping straight into long sessions your legs aren't ready for.

slides.title: Keep jumps low and soft
slides.body: Aim for small, quiet jumps on the balls of your feet with soft knees. You only need to clear the rope by a couple of centimetres.

slides.title: Surface and shoes matter
slides.body: A gym floor, wooden deck or mat is kinder than concrete. Supportive trainers help too. Add slow calf raises twice a week to build capacity in your calves and Achilles.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain in one spot on the shin, pain that's worse each session, pain at rest or at night, or swelling around the Achilles is worth an assessment.

slides.headline: Want to skip without the soreness?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD physios check how your calves, shins and feet handle load, then help you build up gradually. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Picked up the skipping rope for summer fitness? Your calves might be feeling it.

Skipping is quick, effective cardio, but every jump loads your calves, Achilles and shins. Sore legs usually mean you've done too much too soon, not that skipping is bad for you.

Start with short rounds, keep your jumps low and soft, choose a gym floor or mat over concrete, and add calf raises twice a week. Pain in one spot on the shin, pain at rest or at night, or a swollen Achilles is worth getting checked.
